key_insight: Generative AI complicates traditional notions of plagiarism by making idea appropriation easier to commit and harder to prove; the paper argues we need updated definitions, policies, and tools that explicitly address GenAI-driven idea plagiarism.
problem_solved: Clarifies how existing research-misconduct frameworks fail to capture plagiarism of ideas when outputs are produced or mediated by GenAI, and proposes conceptual and policy responses to detect, deter, and adjudicate such cases.
method: Conceptual analysis of current plagiarism and research-misconduct definitions in the context of GenAI
Examination of detection and provenance limits introduced by generative models (e.g., independent convergence, model hallucination, lack of traceability)
Policy and governance recommendations: revise definitions, require transparency/provenance, strengthen recordkeeping, and develop institutional guidance and detection practices
impact: Prompts AI/ML practitioners to adopt provenance-aware workflows, document creative inputs/assistive tools, and support institutional policy changes—reducing ethical risk and preserving research integrity in the GenAI era.
visual_elements: Flowchart showing idea origin pathways: human → human, human → GenAI → human, GenAI → human, with risk/high-ambiguity zones highlighted
Venn diagram comparing types of plagiarism (text, data, ideas) and where GenAI increases ambiguity
Timeline/roadmap for policy actions (immediate practices, mid-term tooling, long-term governance)
Icons representing practical measures: provenance logs, attribution badges, detection tools, and training/education
paper_title: Plagiarism of ideas in the age of generative artificial intelligence
